title: Empirical Validation of Agent-Based Models: Alternatives and Prospects
publisher: Journal of Artificial Societies and Social Simulation (JASSS) 10(2):8; Windrum, Fagiolo, Moneta

key_points.claim: AB models are defined by a bottom-up perspective: macro properties emerge from heterogeneous agents' interactions, in contrast to top-down representative-agent models.
key_points.evidence_quote: aggregate properties are interpreted as emerging out of repeated interactions among simple entities rather than from the consistency requirements of rationality and equilibrium imposed by the modeller

key_points.claim: Agents are boundedly rational, with local and partial rationality rules.
key_points.evidence_quote: one can, at most, impute to agents in AB models some local and partial (both in time and space) principles of rationality, e.g. myopic optimisation rules.

key_points.claim: The paper proposes a taxonomy of AB models with four dimensions, which explains the diversity of validation practice.
key_points.evidence_quote: (1) the nature of the object under study, (2) the goal of the analysis, (3) the nature of the main modelling assumptions, and (4) the method of sensitivity analysis.

key_points.claim: Indirect calibration is a four-step approach: it validates outputs against stylised facts and then restricts the parameter space to the values consistent with those facts.
key_points.evidence_quote: the indirect calibration approach first performs validation, and then indirectly calibrates the model by focusing on the parameters that are consistent with output validation.

key_points.claim: The Werker-Brenner approach calibrates initial conditions and parameter ranges from empirical data. It then validates outputs, possibly with Bayesian inference, to weight the model specifications.
key_points.evidence_quote: Each model specification is assigned a likelihood of being accepted, based on the percentage of 'theoretical realisations' that are compatible with each 'empirical realisation'.

key_points.claim: The history-friendly approach uses specific industry case histories to set parameters, interactions and decision rules. It responds to weak validation in early neo-Schumpeterian models.
key_points.evidence_quote: this approach uses the specific historical case studies of an industry to model parameters, agent interactions, and agent decision rules.

key_points.claim: Empirical validation of AB models has no consensus. Six core issues are identified and several problems remain unresolved.
key_points.evidence_quote: Six core issues associated with empirical validation were identified. There is no consensus on how these issues have to be tackled.

key_points.claim: Early AB validation was weak, often only a cursory comparison of a few runs with stylised facts.
key_points.evidence_quote: Empirical validation, when carried out, tended to consist of little more than a cursory comparison of outputs generated by a handful of simulation runs with some very general stylised facts.

reliability_notes: Full text was fetched from a peer-reviewed journal (JASSS, 2007). It is a methodological review focused on AB economics, though the authors say it applies to all AB modelling. It is somewhat dated, and I read only selected sections (introduction, section 4 and the conclusion).
